Our previous projects include OSINT-based analysis of industrial networks and data-driven investment strategy modeling

We focus on ML, data analysis, optimization, and building working prototypes under tight deadlines. We're interested in connecting with people skilled in GIS, visualization, and space science.
summary:
Tellus is a free web tool that turns students and curious citizens into Earth-science "data detectives". You start from a question in plain words, such as "Is the soil in southern Ukraine drying out?", choose a variable and a region, and get a trend map, a time series since 1981 with the seasonal cycle removed, and a verdict in plain language: how fast the variable is changing per decade, the range we are 95% sure about, and how strong the evidence is. When the evidence is weak, the tool says so honestly and estimates how many more years of data would be needed.   
   
It answers the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. It also shows the challenge's key idea: the same variable can trend in opposite directions in different regions. Climate data carry month-to-month "memory", and our significance tests are corrected for it, so the tool does not raise false alarms. It is built on NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 reanalysis) and needs no login and no code.
details:
Tellus

You've heard it many times: "summers are hotter now", "it rains less than it used to". The data to check this are public, but they are hard to use. The variable names are cryptic, the files are huge, and the statistics are easy to get wrong.

One common mistake: climate data have memory. A dry July is often followed by a dry August. A simple trend line ignores this, so it finds "significant" changes much more often than it should.

Tellus does the maths carefully and gives the answer in plain words. Sometimes that answer is "we can't tell yet".

Live: https://talokin1.github.io/tellus/

Code: https://github.com/talokin1/tellus

What you can do

See the whole planet

Choose one of 14 variables: air temperature, precipitation, soil wetness, evaporation, water vapour, snow cover, snow depth, sea ice, sunlight, haze, ozone, satellite rainfall, and two satellite (AIRS) records.

Each square on the map shows how fast that variable changed per decade since 1981:

  • bright colour: the trend is real (it passed a map-wide test against false alarms)
  • greyish: it could be chance
  • hatched: not enough data

You can also look at one season, hide unclear squares, or see where a place changes faster or slower than the world as a whole.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Trend map: air temperature, 1981–2025" ]

Click a country or region

There are 152 countries, 42 IPCC world regions and 5 ready-made regions. A side panel shows:

  • the rate of change and its 95% range
  • how strong the evidence is: no clear trend, a hint, evidence, or strong evidence
  • a chart by year
  • one sentence that sums it up

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Ukraine, air temperature: +0.54 °C per decade, strong evidence" ]

Open the full analysis

The "Full analysis" page shows everything we know about the place:

  • the record without seasonal ups and downs, with a trend line
  • a map of the area
  • the year when the change became bigger than a normal year-to-year swing
  • results by season and by month
  • extreme months and the total change
  • downloads in CSV, PNG and JSON

Next to each result there is a "How do we know?" link with the exact numbers and the test behind it.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Investigation page: Is Ukraine getting warmer?" ]

Get "not proven" when that's the answer

If the data can't tell a trend apart from natural swings, Tellus says so and shows which rates are still possible.

Example: is the soil in southern Ukraine drying out? So far, no clear trend. The data don't support the claim yet.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Southern Ukraine, soil wetness: no clear trend yet" ]

Compare a place with the world

Ukraine warms by +0.54 °C per decade. The world average is +0.17. The gap is +0.38 (95% range: +0.22 to +0.54).

We only say "faster" or "slower" when that gap has a trend of its own, month by month.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Ukraine compared with the world average, by season" ]

Compare two regions

The same variable can go up in one region and down in another. To check whether two regions really differ, Tellus tests the trend of the difference between them. Comparing two separate p-values is not enough.

Example: is northern Europe getting wetter while the south gets drier? Not clearly, at least not yet (p = 0.42).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Precipitation, clear trends only, with prepared regions compared" ]

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Compare two regions: Southern vs Northern Europe" ]

Look deeper

For the 5 ready-made regions we also use daily data. That gives things people actually notice:

  • summer days above 25 °C and frost nights
  • the hottest day and the coldest night of the year
  • length of the growing season and the last spring frost
  • drought indices (SPI and SPEI)

The main trend is also checked four more ways: block bootstrap, first half vs second half of the record, size of year-to-year swings, and a test for a sudden jump (for example, after an instrument change). Rows where nothing changed are shown too.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Deeper checks for Ukraine" ]

Draw your own area

Use "Draw an area" to mark any box on land or sea. It is tested in the browser with the same methods. Draw a second box to see if the two places really change differently.

If you draw a box around the strangest spot you found on the map, Tellus warns you: this is a lead, not proof.

Ask the assistant

Ask in English or Ukrainian what a result means, how a test works, or where else to look. The assistant (Google Gemini) uses the numbers the app already computed. It links to the right pages and can draw charts from our data. If it searches the web, it lists the sources.

Answers are marked as AI-generated. The verdict card and the Methods page are the main reference.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The assistant explaining a result" ]

Browse the catalog

Each variable has a one-line definition and a short note on why it might change. You can filter by topic or by type of place: farmland and steppe, cities, deserts, forests, cold places, mountains, coasts, tropics.

The catalog also lists 14 more NASA variables that are not on the map yet.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Catalog of variables" ]

How it works

Every number on the site comes from one open-source pipeline:

  1. Average the region. Take the grid squares inside the border. Squares near the poles are smaller, so they count less (weighted by cos latitude).
  2. Remove the seasons. Compare January with January, July with July.
  3. Measure the trend. Change per decade with a 95% range (Sen's slope). A few odd months can't pull it around.
  4. Test it. We run two independent tests: Mann–Kendall with the Yue–Wang correction for memory, and a regression test with an effective sample size. If they disagree, we report the weaker result.
  5. Make sure it holds. We repeat the test without the first two years, without the last two, and on yearly averages. The headline uses the most cautious result.
  6. Avoid false finds on maps. When many tests run at once (map squares, months, seasons, extremes), we use the Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q = 0.05).
  7. Put it into words. The sentences come from fixed templates, so the text never sounds stronger than the test. If there is no clear trend, we estimate how many more years of data would be needed.

Why the memory correction matters. We tested thousands of simulated records with no trend but with realistic memory. The classic Mann–Kendall test raised false alarms up to 33% of the time. Ours stayed between 3% and 6%, close to the expected 5%.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"False-alarm rate of different trend tests" ]

We downloaded the data from the NASA POWER archive on AWS Open Data and keep a fixed copy. Every file has a checksum and a record of where it came from.

Who it's for

  • Teachers and students can check an everyday claim against 40+ years of data in one lesson and learn what "significant" really means.
  • Journalists and readers can see if a trend is real before repeating a headline.
  • Local officials can see if their region changes faster than the world, in which season, and how certain that is.

What's different

  • You get an answer with an evidence level, not just a chart. Each sentence links to the test behind it.
  • "Not proven yet" is a normal result, along with how many more years it might take.
  • Two regions are compared by testing their difference, not by looking at two charts.
  • The statistics account for memory in climate data and use two tests plus stability checks.
  • The assistant works from the app's own numbers
